anatomy.lede: The harpy eagle is built to hunt inside the forest rather than above it: short, broad wings and a long tail for steering between trees, an owl-like face for listening, and feet strong enough to seize a sloth.

hotspots.label: Crest
hotspots.text: A crest of long feathers can be raised and lowered at will, for example when the eagle feels threatened.

hotspots.label: Facial disc
hotspots.text: A ring of feathers around the face can be lifted to funnel sound towards the ears on the sides of the head — a trait shared with owls.

hotspots.label: Bill
hotspots.text: The hooked black bill tears meat; a mother feeds her tiny chick small pieces with it.

hotspots.label: Chest band
hotspots.text: Adults have a dark band across the chest above a white belly. This colouring may help eagles recognise mates that are ready to breed.

hotspots.label: Wing
hotspots.text: Harpies are not built for soaring. Their relatively short wings let them fly from tree to tree with surprising agility for their size.

hotspots.label: Legs
hotspots.text: Thick, powerful legs let the eagle snatch prey from the canopy and carry it off to a perch.

hotspots.label: Talons
hotspots.text: The rear talons are about 8–10 cm long — the size of a grizzly bear's claws.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: The long, barred tail acts like a rudder for steering through dense vegetation.

senses.lede: Under the canopy, even at midday, the forest is dim. The harpy hunts with both eyes and ears.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Harpies use keen eyesight to find prey in thick rainforest, sometimes dropping below the canopy to search.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Because little light reaches the forest interior, harpies also use hearing to pinpoint prey, raising the feathers of the facial disc to direct sound to their ears.

body.lede: A predator of monkeys and sloths needs immense grip, precise flight in cramped spaces and a gut that copes with irregular meals.

systems.title: Feet for heavy prey
systems.text: Powerful legs and long, sharp talons let harpies catch animals that are out of reach for most birds, including howler monkeys, sloths and even young deer.

systems.title: Steering, not soaring
systems.text: Short wings and a long tail suit slow travel from tree to tree rather than long flights over open country.

systems.title: Feast and wait
systems.text: Harpies do not hunt every day. They may feed on one kill for several days and tolerate slightly rotten meat.

genome.lede: A chromosome-level harpy eagle genome was produced by the Vertebrate Genomes Project in 2022. Its chromosomes had already shown how unusual birds of prey are.

findings.title: A reshuffled karyotype
findings.text: Most birds have a few large chromosomes and many tiny 'microchromosomes'. Painting harpy chromosomes with chicken probes showed this pattern has been lost: they are mostly medium-sized, with only four pairs as small as chicken microchromosomes.

mind.lede: Long-lived and slow-breeding, harpies form stable partnerships and invest heavily in a single chick.

studies.title: Partners for life
studies.text: Pairs build the nest together, chirping to each other, and occasionally rub their bills together for a few seconds — behaviour thought to strengthen their bond.

studies.title: Fresh greenery
studies.text: Adults keep bringing green twigs to the nest after the chick hatches. Some researchers think this keeps insects and parasites away or cools the nest.

studies.title: Patient hunters
studies.text: A harpy can stay perched for up to 23 hours while watching for prey.

survival.lede: As an apex predator, an adult harpy has no natural enemies. Its fate is tied to the forest.

tactics.title: Careful with dangerous prey
tactics.text: Monkeys and sloths can fight back with teeth and claws, and young eagles in particular risk injury while learning to hunt.

tactics.title: Guarding the nest
tactics.text: Parents defend the nest and their territory of about 30 km², driving out competing eagles.

threats.title: Forest loss
threats.text: Logging and farming destroy the tall forest harpies need; where too much forest is cleared, parents cannot feed their young.

threats.title: Shooting
threats.text: Harpies are shot by people who fear them or think they take livestock. A 2002 survey in Panama found most killings stemmed from misunderstanding the bird's behaviour.

life.lede: Raising one harpy takes so long that a pair usually breeds only every two to three years.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The female lays one or two eggs and does most of the incubating, but only one chick is raised; the second egg may be a back-up.

stages.name: Nestling
stages.text: A hatchling fits in the palm of a hand, yet reaches adult size in five or six months, when it fledges.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: The young eagle stays dependent on its parents for one to two years, then disperses to find its own territory.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Young birds are pale grey and white, darkening with each moult until they reach adult plumage at about five years old.
